function.name: telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get
function.description: Retrieves specified telemetry information for a network interface within a given fabric, node, and pod, filtered by the interface and information types. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

fabricName.description: The name of the fabric to limit the nodes pertaining to the given fabric name.

nodeId.description: The identifier of the node to limit the results pertaining to the given node ID.

podId.description: The identifier of the pod to limit the results pertaining to the given pod ID.

interfaceType.description: The type of the interface to limit the results pertaining to the given interface type.

infoType.description: The type of information to retrieve about the interface.

message.content:
Below is a quick “recipe” for pulling interface‑level telemetry for a specific node in the **test‑de** fabric. Because the function you have available (`telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get`) works on a *node* and a *pod*, you’ll first need to map the IP address you mentioned (23.31.32.1) to the corresponding **nodeId** and **podId**. Once you have those IDs you can call the function exactly as shown. --- ## 1️⃣ Map the IP → nodeId / podId | What you have | What you need | How to find it | |---------------|---------------|----------------| | IP address (23.31.32.1) | `nodeId` (numeric) | • Query the fabric’s inventory API (e.g., `/api/fabric/test-de/nodes`) and filter by IP.
• Or look up the node in your network management UI and note its numeric ID. | | – | `podId` (numeric) | • Usually the same as the node’s pod number; check the same inventory endpoint or UI. | > **Tip:** If you’re using a CLI or SDK that already knows the mapping, you can often do something like: > ```bash > curl -s http:///api/fabric/test-de/nodes | jq '.[] | select(.ip=="23.31.32.1") | {nodeId, podId}' > ``` --- ## 2️⃣ Call the telemetry function Once you have the IDs, you can pull the telemetry you’re interested in. Below is a Python‑style snippet that demonstrates the call: ```python from functions import telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get # Replace these with the actual IDs you discovered fabric_name = "test-de" node_id = pod_id = # Example: Get all Ethernet interfaces and their status result = telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get( fabricName=fabric_name, nodeId=node_id, podId=pod_id, interfaceType="ethernet", # choose "svi", "loopback", "port-channel" if needed infoType="interfaces" # or "status", "statistics", "errors" ) print(result) ``` ### What each parameter means | Parameter | Description | Allowed values | |-----------|-------------|----------------| | `fabricName` | Name of the fabric you’re querying | `"test-de"` | | `nodeId` | Numeric ID of the node (not the IP) | e.g., `42` | | `podId` | Numeric ID of the pod containing the node | e.g., `1` | | `interfaceType` | Which interface family to limit the query to | `"svi"`, `"ethernet"`, `"loopback"`, `"port-channel"` | | `infoType` | What kind of telemetry you want | `"interfaces"`, `"status"`, `"statistics"`, `"errors"` | --- ## 3️⃣ Interpreting the result The function returns a JSON‑like structure (depending on your SDK). For example, if you requested `"interfaces"` you might see: ```json { "interfaces": [ { "name": "Ethernet1/1", "status": "up", "statistics": { ... }, "errors": { ... } }, ... ] } ``` If you requested `"status"` you’ll get a flat list of status objects, and so on. --- ## 4️⃣ Quick sanity check If you’re unsure whether the IDs you found are correct, you can do a quick sanity check by calling the function with `infoType="interfaces"` and verifying that the returned interface names match what you expect for the node at 23.31.32.1. --- ### Need help finding the nodeId/podId? If you don’t have an inventory API handy, let me know and I can walk you through a typical command‑line approach (e.g., using `curl` + `jq` or a network‑management CLI). Once you have those IDs, just plug them into the snippet above and you’ll get the telemetry you need.
